core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Hyperparathyroidism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming PTH-dependent hypercalcemia biochemically before pursuing parathyroid localization imaging or surgical referral, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe bone pain, fatigue, and recurrent kidney stones over the past year

Key HPI features: 51F presents with chronic aching bone pain in legs and back, generalized fatigue, and history of 2 painful kidney stone episodes in the past year. Also reports mild depression and abdominal discomfort.

Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Primary Hyperparathyroidism (manifesting as 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones').
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Hyperparathyroidism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe confusion.
management_principles: Check serum calcium, albumin, intact PTH, phosphate, and 24-hour urine calcium to confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia
Use neck ultrasound or other localization imaging only after biochemical diagnosis and a decision to pursue parathyroid surgery; imaging does not establish the diagnosis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 51F presenting with a one-year history of chronic aching bone pain in the legs and back, recurrent kidney stones (2 episodes), generalized fatigue, mild depression, and abdominal discomfort — a symptom complex classically described as 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones.'
reference_soap.objective: Vitals and general exam without acute distress. Assess for signs of chronic hypercalcemia and check for neck masses. Labs: elevated serum calcium, elevated or inappropriately normal intact PTH, low-normal or low phosphate, and elevated 24-hour urine calcium; renal ultrasound to assess for nephrolithiasis and bone density (DXA) for skeletal involvement.
reference_soap.assessment: Primary Hyperparathyroidism, given the recurrent kidney stones, chronic bone pain, fatigue, depression, and abdominal discomfort — the classic 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones' presentation.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm PTH-dependent hypercalcemia with repeat calcium (albumin-corrected or ionized) and intact PTH; assess renal function, phosphate, vitamin D, bone density, and 24-hour urine calcium to help exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Use neck localization imaging only after biochemical diagnosis and a decision to pursue surgery. Refer to Endocrinology and endocrine surgery because nephrolithiasis is a surgical indication.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Primary Hyperparathyroidism (manifesting as 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones').

Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for endocrinology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Primary Hyperparathyroidism (manifesting as 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones').

teaching.one_liner: Excess PTH causing the classic tetrad of bone pain, kidney stones, GI symptoms, and depression from chronic hypercalcemia.

must_ask.say: How many kidney stone episodes have you had?
Have you felt depressed or constipated?
How long has this been going on?

history.answer: For the past year, my bones have been aching all over, I feel completely exhausted, and I've had two painful kidney stone attacks.
The deep aching in my bones and this heavy tiredness crept up slowly about a year ago, and it's been getting gradually worse.
The aching is mainly in my lower back and down both of my legs, especially along my shin bones.
It feels like a deep, dull ache right inside my bones, around a four or five out of ten on most days.
The bone ache is pretty much constant every single day, while the kidney stone episodes were sudden, agonizing spasms that lasted hours.
Walking or standing for too long makes the aching worse, and sitting down helps a bit, but the ache never completely goes away.
I had two severe bouts of flank pain in the past year, one eight months ago and one two months ago, both diagnosed as kidney stones.
I feel worn out and drained no matter how much rest I get, and my legs feel heavy when climbing stairs.
I've been feeling down, irritable, and just not like myself lately, which is really unusual for me.
I've had a vague, dull belly ache and nagging constipation that started around the same time as the tiredness.
Now that you mention it, I find myself thirsty all the time, and I have to get up twice every night to urinate.
No, I haven't been confused or disoriented, although I feel a bit foggy because I'm so exhausted.
No, I haven't had any fevers, chills, or night sweats.
No, my weight has been steady and I haven't noticed any unintentional weight loss.
I get a little mild nausea from time to time, but I haven't vomited.
At the emergency room for the stones, they gave me IV fluids and pain shots, and for the second stone they used shock waves to break it up.
I tried taking acetaminophen for the body aches, but it barely made a dent.
I eat regular home-cooked meals, and I don't take any calcium tablets, antacids, or extra vitamin supplements.
It has made keeping up with household chores very hard, and I often have to lie down and rest midway through the day.
I was wondering if I might have developed severe osteoporosis or maybe chronic fatigue syndrome.
I'm terrified of going through another excruciating kidney stone attack.
I was hoping we could check my calcium and vitamin levels to find out what is causing all this.
Aside from the two kidney stone attacks over the past year, I have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic illnesses.
I've never had major surgery, just the shock-wave procedure six months ago to break up my kidney stone.
I am not taking any regular prescription medications right now.
I have no allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink alcohol.
I am a homemaker and live at home with my husband.
No one in my family has had kidney stones, calcium issues, or any glandular tumors.
My periods stopped naturally about two years ago, so I am completely through menopause.
No, there is no chance of pregnancy since I am postmenopausal.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 126/80 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and oriented woman in no acute distress, appearing mildly weary.
No palpable lymphadenopathy in the anterior or posterior cervical chains.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and non-tender, with no palpable neck masses or parathyroid enlargement.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without crackles or wheezes.
Soft and non-distended with vague diffuse mild tenderness, but no guarding, rigidity, or focal tenderness.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either side.
Mild tenderness on deep palpation over the lumbar spine and anterior mid-tibiae; straight-leg raise test is negative.
Normal range of motion in all major joints without swelling, warmth, or deformity.
Alert, fully oriented to time, place, and person, with intact cognition and mildly subdued affect.
Normal tone and 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities, with mild proximal muscle fatigue on repetitive testing.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric at the biceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons; plantar responses are flexor.
